items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: I don’t know why Blue Note wants to recreate Art Blakey’s sound. You can’t. There’s no players that can — they can duplicate it but the feeling’s not there.

ctx.x: All right. I’ll be checking it out. And do you hear artists out there these days that you think are doing anything new?

That’s difficult for me to say because first of all, [sings] don’t get around much anymore. But if I do I’m on the outskirts of town. But just listening to the records or CD’s, or things, unfortunately no. Because I don’t know why Blue Note wants to recreate Art Blakey’s sound. You can’t. There’s no players that can — they can duplicate it but the feeling’s not there. So why not let these new, young artists do their own thing? You know what I mean? Give them their own voice. And therefore that question is…

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: later on man, we became very close. We were good friends but man he turned me completely around.

ctx.x: Did you go back and say man, what are you doing?

No, I just -- you know, how are you doing man? And then later on man, we became very close. We were good friends but man he turned me completely around. And he knew he did it. Man, it was like -- here again man, I ended up -- I only play me. I don’t know anybody else that plays like I do, whether it’s bad, or good, or indifferent. When I’m playing I’m doing the best I can. It might sound terrible, but I’m doing the best I can, you dig? Which is the way I like it, you know. But anyway that’s what started it, and…
Okay, so you’ve now moved to New York. No, you’re still in LA.
